dateConvention: Dates are Julian, as Byzantine sources and modern reference works give them. Cards follow the senior emperor; co-emperors crowned as children appear on their senior's card. reigns.tagline: The teenage emperor everyone else ruled for him
reigns.previously: Theodosius I is dead. The empire is split for good between his sons.
paragraphs: On 17 January 395 Theodosius I died at Milan, and the Roman world split down the middle. His younger son Honorius got the West. The elder, Arcadius, about 17, got the East, with its capital at Constantinople. Nobody ever put the two halves back together. Arcadius was quiet, sleepy-eyed and easy to steer, and for thirteen years a string of strong personalities did the steering.

First came the prefect Rufinus, hacked to pieces by Gainas's soldiers on parade that November. Then the eunuch Eutropius, who ruled the court until his fall in 399. Then Gainas himself, a Gothic general who held the city until a rising in 400 drove his Goths out. Last came the empress Eudoxia, who feuded with the fiery preacher John Chrysostom until he was sent into exile in 404.
Eudoxia died that same year. Arcadius followed on 1 May 408, aged about 31. He left one son, Theodosius, who was just seven.

claims.text: Arcadius asked the Persian king Yazdegerd I to act as guardian to his little son.
claims.note: Procopius tells it more than a century later. No earlier writer mentions it, though peace with Persia did hold.

claims.text: Chrysostom compared Eudoxia to Jezebel and Herodias in his sermons.
claims.note: The church historians Socrates and Sozomen report it. Some of the sermons quoted were probably not his.

claims.text: Thousands of Goths were burned to death in a church when Gainas's men were driven out.
claims.note: Several writers of the time describe the massacre, though their numbers vary.

reigns.hook: The emperor of the East is a boy of seven. Who will really rule? A tough prefect, and then the boy's own big sister.

reigns.tagline: The bookish boy-king behind the greatest walls on earth
reigns.previously: Arcadius is dead, leaving a seven-year-old son on the throne.
paragraphs: Theodosius II reigned for 42 years and hardly ever ruled. As a boy he had the prefect Anthemius, who built the great land walls of Constantinople, finished in 413. Then his big sister Pulcheria, made Augusta in 414, took charge of the palace and ran it like a convent. He grew up gentle, pious and fond of copying books in a beautiful hand, hence his nickname.

In 421 he married Athenais, the clever daughter of a pagan teacher from Athens, renamed Eudocia. In 438 came the Theodosian Code, a great collection of Roman laws. But the Huns under Attila were growing fat on tribute paid by Constantinople. When an earthquake brought the walls down in 447 with Attila on the move, the city's people rebuilt them in a frantic rush.

Church rows filled the rest: councils at Ephesus in 431 and again in 449, the second so violent it was called the Robber Council. In July 450 he fell from his horse while out riding and died two days later. He had no son.

claims.text: The walls were rebuilt in about two months after the 447 earthquake.
claims.note: A Latin inscription still on the walls boasts they were finished in under two months. Boast or not, it was certainly fast.

claims.text: Theodosius gave Eudocia a giant apple, she gave it to his friend Paulinus, and it came back to him, ruining her.
claims.note: The tale comes from John Malalas, a century later. Paulinus was executed and Eudocia did retire to Jerusalem, but the apple is folklore.

claims.text: Pulcheria and her sisters took public vows of virginity.
claims.note: Sozomen, writing during the reign, reports it, and Pulcheria's vow mattered again when she married.

reigns.hook: No son, and Attila wants his gold. Pulcheria needs a husband in name only, and the general Aspar has just the man.

reigns.tagline: The old soldier who told Attila no
reigns.previously: Theodosius II is dead after a riding fall, with no son to follow him.
paragraphs: Marcian was a plain, elderly officer who had served under the powerful general Aspar. When Theodosius died, Aspar backed him and Pulcheria agreed to marry him, which gave him the family link he needed. She was in her fifties and had sworn to stay a virgin. He promised to respect that.

Then he did something bold. Attila's envoys came for the usual tribute and Marcian refused to pay. Attila turned west instead, into Gaul and Italy, and in 453 he died on his wedding night. In 451 Marcian hosted the Council of Chalcedon, which set out what most Christians still believe about Christ's nature. It also split the eastern churches for good.
He was careful with money, and he left the treasury full when he died in January 457. He had no son, and once again Aspar would choose the next emperor.

claims.text: On the night Attila died, Marcian dreamed he saw Attila's bow broken.
claims.note: Jordanes tells it, citing the historian Priscus. A neat omen story, written down after the fact.

claims.text: Pulcheria's marriage to Marcian was never consummated.
claims.note: Church writers praise her for keeping her vow. Nobody at the time suggested otherwise, though we only have their word.

reigns.hook: Aspar is the most powerful man in the empire, but as an Arian and a barbarian he can't take the crown himself. So he picks someone he thinks he can control.

reigns.tagline: The puppet who cut his own strings
reigns.previously: Marcian is dead, and Aspar is choosing the next emperor.
paragraphs: Aspar was an Alan and an Arian Christian, which ruled him out of the throne. So he put up Leo, a Balkan officer in his service, expecting a grateful puppet. Leo had other ideas. He needed his own muscle, so he recruited tough highlanders from Isauria in southern Asia Minor. Their chief, Tarasikodissa, took the name Zeno and married Leo's daughter Ariadne.

In 468 Leo threw a vast fleet at the Vandals in Africa under his wife's brother Basiliscus. Off Cape Bon the Vandals sent in fireships and the armada burned. The cost almost emptied the treasury. Then, in 471, Leo had Aspar and his son cut down inside the palace. People called him Makelles, "the Butcher".
When he died in January 474 the crown went to his grandson Leo II, Zeno and Ariadne's little boy, aged about six or seven.

claims.text: Leo was the first emperor crowned by the patriarch of Constantinople.
claims.note: Later Byzantine writers say so, but the earliest accounts don't clearly mention the patriarch, and the ceremony grew up slowly.

claims.text: The Vandal expedition cost 130,000 pounds of gold.
claims.note: That is Procopius's figure. Other writers give about 64,000 pounds of gold plus silver. Either way it was ruinous.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is a small boy, and his father is an Isaurian chieftain the capital despises. The boy's first act is to crown his dad.

reigns.tagline: The Isaurian who lost his throne, then got it back
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned by his own little son
reigns.previously: Leo I is dead. His grandson, a small boy, is emperor.
paragraphs: On 29 January 474 the child emperor Leo II crowned his father Zeno as co-emperor. By November the boy was dead and Zeno ruled alone. The capital never warmed to him: he was an Isaurian, a highlander born Tarasikodissa. In January 475 Basiliscus, Leo I's brother-in-law, seized the city and Zeno fled to the hills of home.

Basiliscus made himself hated fast, and in August 476 Zeno marched back in. He sent Basiliscus and his family off to Cappadocia, where they died. That same year, in Italy, Odoacer deposed the last western emperor and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. One emperor was enough, he said.

Zeno tried to calm the church with a compromise, the Henotikon of 482, which angered Rome instead. In 488 he solved his Gothic problem by sending Theodoric and the Ostrogoths off to conquer Italy. He died in April 491 without a surviving son.

claims.text: Basiliscus and his family were shut up and left to die of cold and hunger.
claims.note: Several chroniclers agree they died of exposure and starvation in Cappadocia, though they differ on the place.

claims.text: Ariadne had Zeno buried alive while he was in a drunken or epileptic stupor, and he was heard calling from the tomb.
claims.note: Only much later chroniclers such as Kedrenos and Zonaras tell this. Writers closer to the time say he died of illness.

reigns.hook: Zeno is gone and the widowed empress Ariadne gets to choose. She picks a grey-haired palace official, and then she marries him.

reigns.tagline: The penny-pinching clerk who filled the treasury
reigns.previously: Zeno is dead, and his widow Ariadne must choose the next emperor.
paragraphs: Anastasius was a palace usher, about 60, respected and tidy-minded. Ariadne chose him and married him a few weeks later. He threw Zeno's Isaurian cronies out of the capital, which started a war in Isauria that dragged on from 492 to 497. He won it.

Then he got to work on money. In 498 he brought in a new copper coinage people could actually trust, and he abolished the hated chrysargyron, a tax on traders that even prostitutes had to pay. He built the Long Walls across Thrace to guard the city's hinterland. His church views were less popular. Riots over the creed broke out in the Hippodrome, and the general Vitalian rose in revolt and marched on the capital more than once.
He died in 518 at about 88, leaving a huge treasury and three nephews. He never named any of them as heir.

claims.text: Anastasius had one blue eye and one black, and was nicknamed Dikoros.
claims.note: Byzantine chroniclers describe his odd eyes and use the nickname. Hard to check, but nobody seems to have invented it to mock him.

claims.text: He left a treasury of 320,000 pounds of gold.
claims.note: The figure comes from Procopius's Secret History, written to show how fast Justinian spent it.

claims.text: When the creed riots peaked in 512, he appeared in the Hippodrome without his crown and offered to step down. The crowd backed off.
claims.note: Reported by Marcellinus Comes and others writing soon after.

reigns.hook: No heir, a full treasury and a palace in panic. The man in charge of the palace guard is a Balkan peasant who can barely read.

reigns.tagline: The swineherd who walked into the palace
reigns.previously: Anastasius is dead at 88, with no heir named.
paragraphs: Justin was a peasant from the Balkans who had come to Constantinople as a young man to join the army. Fifty years later he commanded the Excubitors, the palace guard. When Anastasius died, the court argued for a day, and the old soldier came out on top. He was about 68.

He was no scholar, but he was no fool either. He had brought his clever nephew Petrus Sabbatius to the capital, educated him and adopted him. The nephew became Justinian, and soon he was steering policy. In 519 Justin ended a 35-year split with the pope. Later he changed the law so that a senator could marry a former actress. That was for Justinian, who was in love with Theodora.
On 1 April 527 Justin made Justinian co-emperor. Four months later he died, worn down by an ulcer from an old wound.

claims.text: Justin walked to Constantinople with two friends and nothing but some bread in their packs.
claims.note: Procopius tells it in his Secret History, which is out to sneer at the family. The poor-boy origin itself is not in doubt.

claims.text: Justin couldn't write and signed documents by tracing letters through a wooden stencil.
claims.note: Again the Secret History. Possible, but Procopius wanted the dynasty to look ridiculous.

claims.text: He was given money to bribe the guards for another candidate and used it to win the throne himself.
claims.note: Several chroniclers tell it. It fits the facts, but no one can prove it.

reigns.hook: The old soldier is dead. His nephew has big ideas, a famous ex-actress for a wife, and nearly four decades to make them happen.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who never slept and wanted it all back
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew and adopted son of Justin I
reigns.previously: Justin I is dead. His nephew Justinian is already co-emperor.
paragraphs: Justinian worked through the night and wanted to rebuild the whole Roman world. His wife Theodora, a former actress, was his equal partner. His lawyers boiled a thousand years of Roman law into one Code (529 to 534) that still underpins law across Europe. In January 532 the Nika riot nearly toppled him. Theodora talked him out of fleeing, and his troops trapped the rioters in the Hippodrome and slaughtered them.

From the ashes rose Hagia Sophia, dedicated on 27 December 537. His general Belisarius took Vandal Africa in 533 to 534, then Italy, entering Ravenna in 540. Then plague struck in 541. Justinian caught it and survived, though huge numbers in the city died. Italy dragged on for years, and Theodora died in 548.
He ruled until November 565, dying at about 83. He had no children, and his sister's son Justin was waiting.

claims.text: Theodora told the panicking court that "royalty is a good burial shroud" and shamed Justinian into staying.
claims.note: Procopius reports the speech in his Wars. He wasn't in the room, and his wording echoes an older Greek saying.

claims.text: On entering Hagia Sophia, Justinian cried, "Solomon, I have outdone you!"
claims.note: First found in a story of the building written centuries later. A great line, but probably invented.

claims.text: Monks smuggled silkworm eggs out of the East in hollow canes, starting a Byzantine silk industry.
claims.note: Procopius reports it in his Wars and a later writer agrees. Details such as the canes are less certain.

reigns.hook: The great man is dead and his conquests are fraying. His nephew Justin takes over with a proud wife and a dangerous plan: stop paying the Persians.

reigns.title: Justin II and Tiberius II
reigns.tagline: A mad emperor, a clever empress and a spendthrift heir
reigns.previously: Justinian is dead at about 83, with no children of his own.
paragraphs: Justin II was Justinian's nephew, and his wife Sophia was Theodora's niece. He was proud and wanted to look strong. In 568 the Lombards poured into Italy, which had barely been won back. In 572 he stopped paying the Persians for peace. The war went badly, and in 573 the great fortress of Dara fell. The shock broke his mind.

Sophia took charge with the commander of the guard, Tiberius. He was made Caesar in 574 and Augustus in September 578. When Justin died that October, Tiberius II Constantine ruled alone. He was handsome and generous to a fault, and he spent the treasury on gifts to the people and the army.
In August 582, struck down by illness, he promised his daughter Constantina to his best general, Maurice, and had him crowned emperor. He died the next day.

claims.text: In his madness Justin was pulled around the palace in a little wagon to calm him, and he bit his servants.
claims.note: John of Ephesus, who lived in the city at the time, describes it. He disliked Justin's religious policy, so he had no reason to be kind.

claims.text: Tiberius found a hoard of gold under a marble slab marked with a cross.
claims.note: Gregory of Tours tells it far away in Gaul. A pious story about a generous king being rewarded.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is a general from Cappadocia with the treasury spent and enemies on every border. He'll fix a lot, and pay dearly for it.

reigns.tagline: The careful general who pushed his army too far
reigns.previously: Tiberius II is dead, after naming Maurice his heir.
paragraphs: Maurice was crowned on 13 August 582 and became sole emperor the next day. He was a general from Cappadocia, hard-working and careful with money, maybe too careful. In 590 the young Persian king Khosrow II was chased off his throne and came begging for help. Maurice put him back, and in 591 got a peace that handed Rome a big slice of Armenia.

Then he turned to the Balkans, where Avars and Slavs had been raiding for years. The wars ground on, and he kept squeezing the troops' pay. In 602 he ordered the army to spend the winter beyond the Danube, in enemy land. The soldiers mutinied and proclaimed a junior officer called Phocas.
Maurice fled across the Bosporus with his family. Phocas's men caught them. On 27 November 602 at Chalcedon, Maurice was made to watch his five sons killed before he was beheaded.

claims.text: Maurice refused to ransom about 12,000 prisoners, and the Avars killed them.
claims.note: Theophylact Simocatta reports it. The number and Maurice's motives are hard to check, but it badly hurt his reputation.

claims.text: A nurse tried to save one of his sons by swapping in her own baby, and Maurice stopped her.
claims.note: Theophylact tells it as a story of saintly fairness. Moving, but it reads like a martyr's tale.

claims.text: Maurice wrote the Strategikon, a famous military handbook.
claims.note: It carries his name and dates from his time. It may have been written by someone else at his court.

reigns.hook: A rough junior officer is now emperor. Far away in Persia, Khosrow II hears that his friend and protector has been murdered.

reigns.tagline: The tyrant who started a war he couldn't win
reigns.previously: Maurice and his sons are dead, killed at Chalcedon.
paragraphs: Phocas was a junior officer the army made emperor. He ruled by fear. Maurice's widow and daughters were killed, generals were burned or blinded, and plot followed plot. Then Khosrow II of Persia invaded in 603, claiming to avenge his friend Maurice. It was the start of the last and greatest war between Rome and Persia, and it went terribly.

In the West Phocas was popular, at least with the pope. In 608 a column with his statue was put up in the Roman Forum. It still stands. He also let the pope turn the Pantheon into a church, which is why it survives today.

But in Carthage the governor of Africa had had enough. In 610 he sent a fleet under his son Heraclius. When it reached Constantinople, the city turned on Phocas. He was dragged before Heraclius and killed on 5 October 610, and his body was cut to pieces.

claims.text: Heraclius asked, "Is this how you ruled?" and Phocas answered, "Will you rule better?"
claims.note: John of Antioch reports the exchange. A perfect last line, and we can't know if it was really said.

claims.text: The Column of Phocas in Rome's Forum was put up in his honour in 608.
claims.note: Its inscription survives, naming Phocas and the exarch Smaragdus who dedicated it.

claims.text: Phocas gave the Pantheon to Pope Boniface IV, who made it a church.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis, the official lives of the popes, records it.

reigns.hook: Heraclius has the throne, but the Persians are pouring into the empire. Jerusalem, Egypt and Constantinople itself are next on their list.

reigns.tagline: He beat Persia, then watched the Arabs take it all
reigns.cameToPower: Sailed from Carthage to topple Phocas
reigns.previously: Phocas is executed and cut to pieces. Young Heraclius takes over.
paragraphs: Heraclius was the son of the governor of Roman Africa, and he arrived to find the empire falling apart. The Persians took Antioch, then Jerusalem in 614, carrying off the True Cross. Egypt, the empire's breadbasket, went in 619. In 626 Avars and Persians camped on both sides of the Bosporus and besieged Constantinople while Heraclius was far away in the East. The city held.

Heraclius had gambled on attacking Persia's heartland. He smashed a Persian army near Nineveh in December 627, and the next year Khosrow II was overthrown and killed by his own people. In 630 Heraclius brought the True Cross back to Jerusalem. Around then he started calling himself basileus, the Greek word for king, and Greek replaced Latin as the language of government. He had also married his own niece, Martina, which shocked the Church.

Then came the Arabs. In 636 they crushed his army at the Yarmouk, and Syria and Jerusalem were gone for good. Heraclius came home a broken, sick old man. He died in February 641, leaving the throne jointly to Constantine III, his son by his first wife, and Heraklonas, his son by Martina.

claims.text: In his last years Heraclius was terrified of water and crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats screened with branches.
claims.note: Told by Patriarch Nikephoros, writing more than a century later. It may be gossip, or a garbled memory of a real illness.

claims.text: His marriage to his niece was cursed, and the ailments of Martina's children were God's punishment.
claims.note: Churchmen and chroniclers said so at the time and after. The marriage was real; the curse is their verdict.

claims.text: Heraclius was the first emperor to use basileus as his official title.
claims.note: It appears in his laws from 629. Greek had long been the everyday language of the East.

reigns.hook: Heraclius leaves the empire to two sons and a widow nobody trusts. Within months one son is dead, and the whispers point straight at Martina.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor who ran away to Sicily
reigns.reignEnded: Killed in his bath at Syracuse
reigns.previously: Heraclius dies, leaving two sons and his widow Martina to share power.
paragraphs: 641 was the year of three emperors. Constantine III died after about three months. Heraklonas and his mother Martina took charge, but the army and the people of the capital hated her. They forced her to crown Constantine III's son, Constans, aged 11. That autumn Heraklonas had his nose slit and Martina her tongue cut out, and both were shipped off to Rhodes.

The boy inherited a disaster. Alexandria fell to the Arabs in 642, and Egypt was lost. In 654 or 655 an Arab fleet beat Constans himself at the Battle of the Masts off the Lycian coast. He fought the Pope too, having Pope Martin I arrested in Rome and exiled to Cherson in the Crimea, where he died. In 660 Constans had his own brother Theodosius killed, and the capital never forgave him.

So he left. Constans moved west, spent twelve days in Rome in 663 and stripped the bronze off its buildings, roof tiles included. He set up court at Syracuse in Sicily. In July 668 a servant attacked him in the bath and killed him. The army in Sicily proclaimed its own emperor, an Armenian officer named Mezezius.

claims.text: Martina poisoned Constantine III to clear the way for her own son.
claims.note: Rumours at the time said so, and later chroniclers repeated them. He had been ill, probably with tuberculosis.

claims.text: The ghost of his murdered brother haunted Constans, offering him a cup of blood and saying, “Drink, brother.”
claims.note: Theophanes tells it, writing about 150 years later. It's a moral tale about a fratricide.

claims.text: The servant killed him by smashing a soap box (or bucket) over his head.
claims.note: Theophanes and later writers give the detail. The bath murder itself is certain; the weapon is the chroniclers' story.

reigns.tagline: Greek fire, angry Arabs and two noseless brothers
reigns.previously: Constans is murdered in his bath at Syracuse. Sicily crowns a rebel.
paragraphs: Constantine's first job was the Sicilian rebel Mezezius, who was crushed within months. Then the Arabs came for Constantinople itself. Through the 670s their fleets raided the Sea of Marmara, wintering at Cyzicus and attacking each summer. The city's secret weapon was Greek fire, a liquid that burned on water, sprayed from tubes on the empire's ships. The Arabs gave up, and in 678 the caliph agreed to pay the empire tribute.

In the Balkans things went worse. In 680 Constantine led an army against the Bulgars of Asparukh, fell ill with gout and left, and his army panicked and was routed. The Bulgars settled south of the Danube and the empire had to pay them. That was the birth of Bulgaria. Back home he ended a long church row: the Sixth Ecumenical Council (680–681) condemned the Monothelete creed his grandfather had backed.

Constantine had two brothers, Heraclius and Tiberius, who were co-emperors in name. In 681 he had their noses slit so they could never rule. He died in 685, aged about 33, leaving the empire to his son Justinian.

claims.text: The Arabs besieged Constantinople for five years, from 674 to 678.
claims.note: That's Theophanes's version. Some recent historians argue it was a run of smaller raids and that the big siege story grew in the retelling.

claims.text: Greek fire was brought to the city by Kallinikos, a refugee architect from Syria.
claims.note: Theophanes says so, writing over a century later. The recipe itself was a state secret and is lost.

claims.text: His troops demanded three emperors to match the Holy Trinity, so Constantine slit his brothers' noses.
claims.note: The Trinity chant is in Theophanes. The brothers' removal is certain: their names vanish from coins and documents in 681.

reigns.hook: Constantine dies young. His son Justinian is 16, clever, hot-tempered and full of grand plans. Nobody yet guesses how far he'll fall, or how he'll climb back.

reigns.tagline: Big plans, bad ministers, and no nose
reigns.previously: Constantine IV dies at about 33. His teenage son inherits the throne.
paragraphs: Justinian II was named after the great Justinian and wanted to live up to it. He campaigned against the Slavs in the Balkans and moved thousands of them into Asia Minor to serve as soldiers. In 692 he marched that army against the Arabs at Sebastopolis. Most of the Slavs deserted to the enemy, and he lost. He took it out on the Slav families left behind.

He was the first emperor to put the face of Christ on his coins, calling himself the servant of Christ. His church council of 692 (the Quinisext) laid down rules the Pope refused to accept. To pay for his building and wars he relied on two hated ministers, the treasurer Stephen the Persian and the logothete Theodotos, who squeezed the rich and poor alike.

In 695 the general Leontios, freshly let out of prison, raised the city and seized Justinian. His nose was cut off, which was meant to make him unfit to rule, since an emperor had to be whole. He was exiled to Cherson in the Crimea. People called him Rhinotmetus, the slit-nosed.

claims.text: Stephen the Persian had the emperor's own mother beaten with a whip while Justinian was away.
claims.note: Only in Theophanes and Nikephoros, who both disliked Justinian. The story shows how hated his ministers were.

claims.text: Justinian's gold coins were the first to show Christ's face.
claims.note: The coins survive in good numbers. Christ is on the front and the emperor on the back.

claims.text: Cutting off his nose was meant to bar him from the throne for good.
claims.note: Byzantines expected an emperor to be physically whole. Mutilation was the standard way to retire a rival without killing him.

reigns.hook: Justinian is noseless, broke and stuck on the edge of the Black Sea. Everyone assumes he's finished. He doesn't agree, and the men who replaced him won't last either.

reigns.title: The Twenty Years' Anarchy
reigns.tagline: Two noseless emperors and an exile with a plan
reigns.reignEnded: Justinian II fought his way back
reigns.previously: Justinian II loses his nose and his throne, and is exiled to Cherson.
paragraphs: Leontios (695–698) had the throne and lost Africa. The Arabs took Carthage in 697. A Byzantine fleet won it back for a moment, then lost it for good in 698. Afraid to go home and face the music, the sailors mutinied and crowned Apsimar, one of their commanders, who took the name Tiberios III (698–705). Leontios had his nose cut off too and went into a monastery.

Meanwhile Justinian was plotting in Cherson. He escaped to the Khazars, whose khagan gave him his sister as a wife, renamed Theodora. When Tiberios bribed the khagan to kill him, she warned him, and Justinian strangled the two men sent to do it. He sailed off, survived a storm, and made a deal with Tervel, khan of the Bulgars.

In 705 Justinian turned up at the walls of Constantinople with a Bulgar army. The city refused to open. After three days he and a few men crept in through an aqueduct, and the city was his. Tiberios fled and was caught.

claims.text: Justinian strangled the two assassins with his own hands.
claims.note: Theophanes and Nikephoros both tell it, but they drew on the same lost source. Hard to check, easy to believe.

claims.text: In the storm he swore that if God spared him, he would spare none of his enemies.
claims.note: Theophanes puts the vow in his mouth. It neatly explains what happened next.

claims.text: He got into the city through an aqueduct.
claims.note: Both chroniclers say he used a water channel. Details of how it was done are unclear.

reigns.hook: Justinian is back on the throne, minus a nose, plus a list of names. Leontios and Tiberios are about to find out how long he's been holding a grudge.

reigns.tagline: The slit-nosed emperor comes back for revenge
reigns.previously: Justinian II creeps back into Constantinople through an aqueduct.
paragraphs: Justinian is the only emperor ever to win his throne back after being mutilated, and he made everyone pay. Leontios and Tiberios were dragged into the Hippodrome, where Justinian sat with his feet on their necks while the crowd watched. Then they were beheaded. The patriarch who had crowned Leontios was blinded. Tervel the Bulgar was rewarded with the title of Caesar, the first foreign ruler to get it.

Justinian brought his Khazar wife Theodora to the capital and crowned their small son Tiberius co-emperor. He sent fleets to punish Ravenna and Cherson, places he felt had wronged him. Cherson rebelled and proclaimed an Armenian officer, Bardanes, as emperor under the name Philippikos.

In 711 Philippikos took Constantinople. Justinian was caught and beheaded, and his head was sent round Rome and Ravenna as proof. His six-year-old son was dragged from a church altar and killed. Heraclius's dynasty, which had ruled for a century, was over.

claims.text: Justinian rested his feet on the necks of Leontios and Tiberios in the Hippodrome.
claims.note: Theophanes and Nikephoros both describe it. Treading on a beaten enemy was an old Roman triumph gesture.

claims.text: Justinian wore a golden nose over his scar.
claims.note: No early source says so. It turns up only in modern retellings.

claims.text: His little son died clinging to the altar with holy relics hung round his neck.
claims.note: Theophanes tells it in moving detail. It may be dressed up, but the boy's killing is not in doubt.

reigns.hook: Justinian's head is on tour in Italy. The new emperor Philippikos likes parties, theology and spending money, and the Arabs have noticed.

reigns.title: Three Emperors in Six Years
reigns.tagline: A party boy, a bureaucrat and a reluctant taxman
reigns.previously: Justinian II is beheaded and his dynasty dies with him.
paragraphs: Philippikos (711–713) brought back the Monothelete creed that the Sixth Council had condemned, while the Bulgars raided up to the walls and the Arabs pushed into Asia Minor. In June 713 soldiers grabbed him in the palace and blinded him.

The court picked a top civil servant, Artemios, who took the name Anastasios II (713–715). He was the sensible one. Expecting a huge Arab attack, he repaired the walls, built up the fleet and told every household to store food for three years or leave the city. But when he sent his fleet against the Arabs in 715, the troops mutinied and proclaimed Theodosios, a tax collector. Theodosios III ran off to hide in the hills, but they dragged him back and made him emperor anyway.
Theodosios lasted until 717. Leo, the general commanding the Anatolikon theme, refused to accept him and marched on the capital. Theodosios stepped down without a fight and became a cleric.

claims.text: Philippikos was seized and blinded while sleeping off a drinking party.
claims.note: Theophanes says he'd lunched well and was having a nap. Theophanes hated him for his creed, so the details may be loaded.

claims.text: Theodosios III fled to the hills to avoid being made emperor.
claims.note: Theophanes's story. Reluctant emperors are a common theme in Byzantine writing.

claims.text: Philippikos tore down the palace image of the Sixth Council and revived Monotheletism.
claims.note: Reported by Byzantine and papal sources, and the Pope refused to recognise him for it.

reigns.hook: Leo the general is at the gates. Behind him, the biggest Arab army and fleet anyone has ever seen are heading for Constantinople.

reigns.tagline: He saved the city from the Arabs, then smashed the icons
reigns.previously: Theodosios III gives up the throne and becomes a cleric.
paragraphs: Leo was born Konon in Germanikeia, in northern Syria. He took the city on 25 March 717, and that summer the Arabs arrived under the caliph's brother Maslama, with a huge army and fleet. Greek fire burned their ships. Then came a terrible winter, with snow lying for months, and the besiegers starved. The Bulgars attacked their camp. In August 718 the Arabs gave up, and storms sank much of their fleet on the way home.

Leo spent the rest of his reign rebuilding. In the 720s he began Iconoclasm, the campaign against holy images, perhaps after a volcanic eruption on Thera convinced him God was angry. The patriarch Germanos resigned rather than go along with it in 730. In 740 Leo and his son Constantine beat an Arab army at Akroinon, a rare victory over them in open battle.
He also issued the Ecloga, a short handbook of Roman law in Greek, with mutilation replacing the death penalty for many crimes. He died in June 741 and his son Constantine succeeded.

claims.text: Leo was an Isaurian.
claims.note: Theophanes says he came from Germanikeia in Syria. The Isaurian label seems to come from a later slip, but it stuck to his dynasty.

claims.text: Leo's men pulled down the icon of Christ over the palace Chalke Gate, and a crowd of women killed the officer doing it.
claims.note: The story is told only in later sources. Some historians think it was invented by iconophiles after the fact.

claims.text: The Ecloga was issued in 726.
claims.note: Its dating clause can be read as 726 or 741. Historians still argue over which.

reigns.hook: Leo dies in his bed. His son Constantine takes over, and within a year his own brother-in-law has stolen the capital out from under him.

reigns.tagline: Hated by the monks, adored by the army
reigns.previously: Leo III dies, the man who saved the city and took down the icons.
paragraphs: His enemies called him Copronymus, the dung-named. The monks who wrote his history loathed him, so we see him through their eyes. In 742 his brother-in-law Artabasdos seized Constantinople while Constantine was marching east, and put the icons back up. Constantine fought his way back and took the city in November 743. Artabasdos and his sons were blinded and paraded in the Hippodrome.

Plague hit in 747 and emptied much of the capital. Constantine refilled it with settlers from Greece and the islands. In the West, Ravenna fell to the Lombards in 751, and Rome began looking to the Franks for protection. In 754 his Council of Hieria banned icons outright, and Constantine turned on the monasteries, which were the icons' strongest defenders.
His soldiers loved him. He led campaign after campaign against Bulgaria and crushed the Bulgars at Anchialos in 763. He died of a fever on campaign in September 775.

claims.text: He got the name Copronymus by soiling the font at his baptism.
claims.note: Told by iconophile writers who hated him. It's an insult dressed up as a story.

claims.text: Constantine forced monks to parade in the Hippodrome, each holding a woman's hand, to mock their vows.
claims.note: Theophanes puts it in 766. He was a monk and a bitter enemy of iconoclasm.

claims.text: His bones were later dug up and burned.
claims.note: Later sources say this happened after icons were restored in the 9th century. The details vary.

reigns.hook: Constantine's son Leo inherits a strong army and a divided Church. His mother was a Khazar princess, and his wife is a young woman from Athens named Irene.

reigns.tagline: Half-Khazar emperor felled by a borrowed crown
reigns.previously: Constantine V dies on campaign against the Bulgars. Leo takes over.
paragraphs: Leo got his nickname from his mother, Tzitzak, a Khazar princess from the steppes north of the Caucasus. She had been married to Constantine V to seal an alliance against the Arabs. In 768 his father found Leo a Greek bride from Athens, a young woman named Irene. Nobody guessed she would one day hold more power than any woman in Roman history.

Leo kept his father's ban on icons but enforced it with a much lighter hand, and the monks breathed a little easier. In 776 he crowned his small son Constantine co-emperor. His half-brothers, led by the Caesar Nikephoros, plotted to take the throne instead. Leo broke the plot and sent the conspirators into exile at Cherson, in the Crimea. On the eastern frontier he traded raids with the Arabs, winning some and losing some.

In September 780 he died of a fever, just 30 years old, after only five years on the throne. His son Constantine was nine. Real power now sat with the widow, Irene, and she had very different ideas about icons.

claims.text: Leo died of boils on his head after taking a jewelled crown from Hagia Sophia and wearing it.
claims.note: Theophanes tells it as God's punishment for greed. He was a monk who loathed the iconoclast emperors, and nobody else confirms it.

claims.text: His mother was a Khazar princess.
claims.note: Theophanes records Constantine V's marriage to the Khazar khagan's daughter, who was baptised Irene; Leo's nickname comes from her.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead at 30 and the new emperor is a boy of nine. Standing beside him is his mother Irene, who means to undo everything her husband's family did to the icons.

reigns.tagline: The emperor his own mother blinded
reigns.reignEnded: Blinded and deposed by his mother
reigns.previously: Leo IV dies of a fever at 30, leaving a son of nine.
paragraphs: Constantine was nine, so his mother Irene ran the empire, and she moved fast. In 787 a church council at Nicaea, the second held there, declared icons holy again and undid half a century of iconoclasm. Constantine had been promised to Charlemagne's daughter Rotrude, but the match fell apart. In 788 Irene chose him a wife herself, a girl from Paphlagonia called Maria.

By 790 Constantine was nearly 20 and tired of taking orders. When the army refused to swear loyalty to Irene first, he took the government into his own hands. It went badly. In 792 the Bulgars routed him, he blinded his uncle Nikephoros to head off a plot, and he let his mother back in as co-ruler. Then he packed Maria off to a convent and married his mistress Theodote. The monks were outraged and his support drained away.

Irene struck in 797. Her men caught Constantine as he tried to flee across the water to Asia, brought him back to the palace, and in August gouged out his eyes. He disappears from the record after that. His mother was now the only ruler of the Roman Empire.

claims.text: Irene picked his wife at a bride show, where officials toured the provinces looking for the most suitable girl.
claims.note: The account comes from the Life of St Philaretos, written by Niketas, Philaretos's grandson and a relative of Maria. Historians argue over whether bride shows really happened like this.

claims.text: He was blinded in the Purple Chamber, the same room where he had been born.
claims.note: Theophanes, writing within about 20 years, gives the detail. It is plausible, but neat enough as poetic justice to make some historians wary.

claims.text: After the blinding the sun went dark for 17 days.
claims.note: Theophanes reports it as a sign of heaven's horror. It reads like a moral comment more than a weather report.

reigns.hook: The blinded emperor vanishes. For the first time a woman rules the Roman Empire alone, and in the West some are about to argue that this means the throne is empty.

reigns.tagline: The first woman to rule Rome alone
reigns.previously: Irene's men blind her son Constantine VI and she takes the throne.
paragraphs: Irene was the first woman to rule the empire on her own, and nobody had a word for it. Her coins called her empress, but some of her laws called her basileus, the male title. To win the crowd she cut taxes and scrapped customs dues. At Easter 799 she rode through the city in a golden chariot drawn by four white horses, tossing coins to the people.

The West was not impressed. On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in Rome. Some Frankish writers said the imperial title was vacant anyway, since a woman held it. Then Charlemagne's envoys turned up in Constantinople, says Theophanes, with an offer of marriage. A wedding would have joined East and West. Irene's ministers were horrified, and they were also busy plotting against each other.

On 31 October 802 her finance minister Nikephoros walked into the palace with a few allies and took over without a fight. Irene was sent to a monastery on an island near the capital, then further away to Lesbos. She died there in August 803. The Orthodox Church later honoured her for bringing back the icons.

claims.text: She used the male title basileus, 'emperor', in some of her laws.
claims.note: It appears in the headings of laws issued in her name, while her coins use the female title. Historians debate how much she meant by it.

claims.text: Charlemagne proposed marriage to Irene.
claims.note: Only Theophanes reports the proposal. Frankish sources record an embassy but say nothing about a wedding.

claims.text: In exile on Lesbos she had to spin wool to pay for her food.
claims.note: Theophanes tells it as a lesson in how far the proud can fall. No other source backs it up.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is a career accountant. Nikephoros will refill the treasury, then march into Bulgaria to settle things with the most dangerous man in the Balkans, the khan Krum.

reigns.tagline: The taxman whose skull became a drinking cup
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by the Bulgars in a pass
reigns.previously: Irene's finance minister seizes the palace and sends her into exile.
paragraphs: Nikephoros had run the treasury, and he ran the empire the same way. He squeezed the Church and the rich, made villages answer for their neighbours' unpaid taxes and forced loans on shipowners. The monk Theophanes, who hated him, listed these as the 'ten vexations'. He also moved settlers into Greece and rebuilt towns there, pulling the Peloponnese firmly back under imperial control.

Abroad things were harder. He stopped paying the tribute Irene had agreed with the caliph Harun al-Rashid, and Harun's armies soon made him pay again. In 811 he invaded Bulgaria and burned the khan Krum's capital at Pliska. Marching home, his army entered a mountain pass that the Bulgars had blocked at both ends. At dawn on 26 July they attacked. Nikephoros was killed along with much of his army.
His son Staurakios was carried out of the pass with a sword wound to his spine. Paralysed and dying, he clung on as emperor for about two months.

claims.text: Krum made Nikephoros's skull into a silver-lined drinking cup and toasted his nobles with it.
claims.note: Theophanes, writing within a few years, reports it, and it fits steppe custom. It is widely believed but cannot be checked.

claims.text: The 'ten vexations' ruined the empire.
claims.note: The list comes from Theophanes, who loathed Nikephoros. Modern historians tend to see the measures as tough but sensible reforms that refilled the treasury.

reigns.hook: Staurakios lasts two months before his sister's husband Michael I Rangabe takes over in 811. Michael lasts two years. Krum is still coming, and an Armenian general named Leo is waiting.

reigns.tagline: The soldier cut down at the Christmas service
reigns.previously: Nikephoros dies in the pass; Michael I Rangabe rules two shaky years.
paragraphs: In June 813 Michael I Rangabe met Krum at Versinikia and lost badly. The army turned to Leo, an Armenian general, and Michael gave up without a fight. He became a monk, and his sons were castrated so they could never rule. One of them later became the Patriarch Ignatios. Within days of Leo's coronation, Krum was camped outside the walls of Constantinople.

Leo invited Krum to talk and hid archers near the meeting place. They missed, and Krum escaped in a fury to ravage Thrace. Then, in April 814, while planning a new assault on the city, Krum suddenly died. Leo made a thirty-year peace with the new khan, Omurtag. In 815 he brought back the ban on icons, sure that it was the iconoclast emperors who had won wars.

His end came from an old comrade, Michael the Amorian. Caught plotting, Michael was condemned to death just before Christmas 820. Before dawn on Christmas Day his friends slipped into the palace chapel dressed as clergy, hiding swords under their robes, and cut Leo down during the service.

claims.text: Leo tried to have Krum killed at a peace parley.
claims.note: Told by Byzantine writers close to the time, who seem to have approved. We have no Bulgarian account.

claims.text: Krum died of a sudden haemorrhage.
claims.note: The cause is given in a short anonymous Byzantine fragment. Nobody can check it.

claims.text: Leo fought off his killers with a heavy cross from the altar until they cut off his arm.
claims.note: The vivid details come from tenth-century chroniclers writing generations later.

reigns.tagline: Crowned in chains, he founded a dynasty
reigns.cameToPower: Leo V murdered by his allies
reigns.previously: Leo V is hacked down at the Christmas service in his palace chapel.
paragraphs: Michael came from Amorion in central Anatolia, a blunt soldier with little schooling. A few hours earlier he had been waiting to die. Now he was emperor, crowned in Hagia Sophia with the iron fetters still on his legs. Leo's widow was sent to a convent, and Leo's sons were castrated and shut away on an island.

Then came the great rebellion. Thomas the Slav, another old comrade from the same army, claimed the throne and won over much of Anatolia. From December 821 he besieged Constantinople by land and sea for over a year. Michael held the walls, the Bulgar khan Omurtag hit Thomas from behind, and in 823 Thomas was caught, his hands and feet were cut off, and he was put to death.

The civil war left the empire exposed. Arab exiles from Spain seized Crete, and in 827 an Arab army landed in Sicily, starting a conquest that would take 75 years. At home Michael kept the ban on icons but did little to enforce it. As a widower he married Euphrosyne, Constantine VI's daughter, taking her out of a convent. His son Theophilos was already co-emperor.

claims.text: He was crowned still wearing his fetters because nobody could find the key.
claims.note: Told by tenth-century chroniclers (Genesios and Theophanes Continuatus). Vivid and plausible, but impossible to check.

claims.text: He spoke with a stammer and could barely read.
claims.note: These details come from histories written for the dynasty that replaced his own, which liked to make the Amorians look crude.

claims.text: Thomas the Slav claimed to be the blinded Constantine VI.
claims.note: Reported by later chroniclers. Historians are unsure how seriously anyone took it.

reigns.hook: Michael dies in his bed in 829, a rare thing lately. His son Theophilos, clever and fond of splendour, now needs a wife, and the empire's finest young women are lined up for him.

reigns.tagline: The last iconoclast and his golden singing birds
reigns.previously: Michael II, crowned in chains, dies in his bed after nine years.
paragraphs: Theophilos's first big decision was his bride. The candidates were lined up and he walked along the row holding a golden apple for the winner. He stopped at Kassia, clever and beautiful, and remarked that through a woman came all evil. Through a woman, she shot back, came better things too. He moved on and gave the apple to Theodora. Kassia founded a convent and became a celebrated hymn writer.

He loved splendour. His throne room had a golden tree full of mechanical birds that sang, with golden lions that roared. He also liked to play the just ruler, riding out each week to hear complaints from anyone in the street. He was the last emperor to ban icons, and the persecution flared again, with monks flogged and branded. Inside the palace, his wife and mother-in-law prayed to icons behind his back.

War with the caliphate turned ugly. Theophilos sacked the town of Zapetra in 837. In 838 the caliph al-Mu'tasim struck back by marching on Amorion, the dynasty's home town, and razing it. Theophilos never really recovered. He died in January 842, aged about 29, leaving a son of two.

claims.text: Kassia's quick answer cost her the crown.
claims.note: The story appears in chronicles written a century or more later. Kassia herself was real and her hymns are still sung.

claims.text: A palace jester caught Theodora kissing her icons and nearly gave her away.
claims.note: From tenth-century histories keen to show Theodora as a secret icon-lover all along.

claims.text: His throne room had singing golden birds and roaring lions.
claims.note: Later chroniclers credit Theophilos with the golden automata. Liudprand of Cremona saw roaring lions and singing birds at the throne in 949, but who built them is less certain.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead and Michael III is two years old. His mother Theodora is regent, and the icons her husband banned are about to come back for good.

reigns.tagline: The 'Drunkard' killed by his drinking companion
reigns.cameToPower: Inherited, with his mother as regent
reigns.previously: Theophilos dies at about 29, leaving a two-year-old son.
paragraphs: Michael was two, so his mother Theodora ran the empire with the eunuch minister Theoktistos. On 11 March 843 she brought the icons back for good, a day the Orthodox Church still marks as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. In 855 Theodora's brother Bardas had Theoktistos murdered, with the teenage emperor's blessing. Theodora was pushed aside and later sent to a convent, and Bardas ran the government.

He ran it well. In 860 a Rus fleet appeared out of nowhere and plundered the outskirts of Constantinople. In 863 the army crushed the emir of Melitene at Lalakaon, a turning point against the Arabs. That year the brothers Cyril and Methodius set off to preach to the Slavs of Moravia, and soon Boris of Bulgaria was baptised. Photios, the most learned man of the age, was patriarch.

Michael, meanwhile, enjoyed himself. His new favourite was Basil, a peasant wrestler and horse-tamer. In 866 Basil killed Bardas in front of the emperor, and Michael made him co-emperor. A year later, on the night of 24 September 867, Basil's men burst into Michael's bedroom after a banquet and cut him down.

claims.text: Michael was a hopeless drunkard.
claims.note: The picture comes from histories written for the family of Basil, his murderer, who needed to justify the killing. Many modern historians see a fairly successful reign.

claims.text: He staged mock church processions with his drinking friends, one dressed up as the patriarch.
claims.note: Told by the same hostile tenth-century histories.

claims.text: The Rus fleet was wrecked by a storm after the Virgin's robe was dipped in the sea.
claims.note: Photios preached about the robe being carried round the walls at the time. The miraculous storm only appears in later writers.

reigns.hook: Basil, a peasant who started out as a groom, is now sole emperor. His family will rule for almost two centuries, and they will make sure Michael is remembered as a drunk.

reigns.tagline: The peasant wrestler who killed his way to the throne
reigns.previously: Basil's men murder Michael III in his bedroom. Basil now rules alone.
paragraphs: Basil was born to a peasant family of Armenian descent in Thrace, a region the Byzantines then called Macedonia. He reached Constantinople with nothing and found work as a groom, where his strength and his way with horses got him noticed. Michael III made him a favourite, then his chamberlain. In 866 Basil killed Michael's uncle Bardas and got himself crowned co-emperor. In September 867 he had Michael murdered.

There was an awkward detail. Michael had married Basil to his own mistress, Eudokia Ingerina, and when her son Leo arrived in 866, people wondered who the father was. As emperor, Basil proved capable. He sacked the patriarch Photios, then later brought him back. He started a vast clean-up of Roman law, and in 880 he consecrated a glittering new palace church, the Nea Ekklesia.

His favourite son, Constantine, died in 879, and Basil never got over it. He grew suspicious of Leo and kept him locked up from 883 to 886. That August Basil was badly hurt out hunting and died days later. The crown went to Leo, the son he trusted least.

claims.text: Basil first caught the emperor's eye by flooring a champion Bulgarian wrestler.
claims.note: Told in the Life of Basil, written at the court of his grandson Constantine VII to make the dynasty's founder look heroic.

claims.text: Leo VI was really Michael III's son, not Basil's.
claims.note: Eudokia was Michael's mistress before and after her marriage to Basil, and Basil treated Leo coldly. Nothing more solid than that survives.

claims.text: A stag hooked Basil's belt with its antlers and dragged him into the forest.
claims.note: Told by later chroniclers. The details may be embroidered, and some historians suspect more than an accident.

reigns.hook: Basil is dead. The new emperor is Leo, the son he locked up and the one whispered to be Michael III's boy. He's clever and bookish, and he is about to have terrible luck with wives.

reigns.tagline: The scholar emperor who married four times
reigns.previously: Basil I dies after a hunting accident. Leo, the son he jailed, rules.
paragraphs: Leo came out of three years in custody and turned into an emperor who loved books. He finished his father's law project as the Basilika, a huge Greek edition of Roman law in sixty books. He wrote a military handbook, the Tactica, and preached his own sermons in church. His brother Alexander was co-emperor, and mostly enjoyed himself.

Leo's marriages were the problem. His first wife, Theophano, died. So did his second, his former mistress Zoe Zaoutzaina, and his third, Eudokia Baïana, in childbirth. No son survived, and the Church frowned even on third marriages. Then his new mistress, Zoe Karbonopsina, “coal-black eyes”, gave him a son, Constantine, born in 905 in the palace's Purple Chamber.

Leo married her in 906, his fourth wedding. The patriarch Nicholas Mystikos refused to accept it and was forced out. Outside the palace things were rough too: Arab raiders sacked Thessalonica in 904, and Simeon of Bulgaria was a dangerous neighbour. Leo died in May 912 with his son still a small child, so his brother Alexander took over.

claims.text: Leo wrote the Oracles of Leo the Wise, riddling prophecies about the empire's fate.
claims.note: The oracles were pinned to his name long after his death, thanks to his reputation for learning.

claims.text: Leo's fourth marriage cost a patriarch his job.
claims.note: Nicholas Mystikos was deposed in 907 for opposing the marriage. He got his job back under Alexander.

claims.text: Thousands of people were carried off as slaves when Thessalonica fell in 904.
claims.note: John Kameniates, one of the captives, wrote an eyewitness account of the sack.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead. His brother Alexander, who never liked him, takes the throne, while Leo's six-year-old son waits in the palace. Simeon of Bulgaria is watching closely.

reigns.title: Constantine VII and Romanos I
reigns.tagline: The boy born in the purple who outlasted everyone
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Leo VI; nephew of Alexander
reigns.previously: Leo VI dies. Brother Alexander rules; little Constantine waits.
paragraphs: Leo's brother Alexander lasted thirteen months. He stopped Bulgaria's tribute, insulted its envoys and died after a game of polo. That left Constantine, aged eight. Simeon of Bulgaria marched to the walls in 913. The patriarch Nicholas Mystikos ran things, then Constantine's mother Zoe pushed him aside, but in 917 her army was crushed by the Bulgarians at Achelous.

In 919 the admiral Romanos Lekapenos sailed in and took charge. He married his daughter Helena to Constantine, then in December 920 crowned himself senior emperor. Romanos was good at the job. He made peace with Bulgaria in 927, burned Prince Igor's Rus fleet with Greek fire in 941, and in 944 brought the Image of Edessa, a cloth said to show Christ's face, to the city.

In December 944 Romanos's own sons deposed him and packed him off to a monastery on the island of Prote. Weeks later Constantine sent the sons there too. From January 945 he ruled alone at last. He wrote, or oversaw, books on foreign peoples and on court ceremony, and welcomed Princess Olga of Kiev to the palace. He died in 959, aged 54.

claims.text: Romanos greeted his sons on Prote with mock delight at their company.
claims.note: Liudprand of Cremona tells it with relish, and he loved a joke at Byzantine expense.

claims.text: Constantine was poisoned by his son Romanos and daughter-in-law Theophano.
claims.note: A rumour reported by later chroniclers. Constantine had been ill, and there is no proof.

claims.text: Olga of Kiev's visit took place in 957.
claims.note: Constantine describes her reception himself in his book on ceremonies, but historians argue over 946 or 957.

reigns.hook: Constantine is dead. His son Romanos, barely 21, inherits with a beautiful wife of mysterious origins and a brilliant general itching to attack Crete.

reigns.tagline: The party prince whose general won the wars
reigns.previously: Constantine VII dies, poison rumoured. His son Romanos inherits.
paragraphs: Romanos II liked hunting, games and good company far more than paperwork. He left the government to the eunuch Joseph Bringas. His wife Theophano was a famous beauty whose birth name was Anastaso, and gossip said her father kept a tavern. Soon after the new couple took over, Romanos's sisters were packed off to convents.

The real star of the reign was the general Nikephoros Phokas. In 960 he sailed for Crete, held by Arab emirs for well over a century, and besieged its capital Chandax through the winter. It fell in March 961. Back in the East, he sacked Aleppo in December 962. Then, in March 963, Romanos died suddenly at 24, leaving two little boys, Basil and Constantine, and a widow in her early twenties.

claims.text: Theophano was an innkeeper's daughter.
claims.note: Later chroniclers, all hostile to her, say so. Her family is otherwise unknown.

claims.text: Romanos was poisoned, perhaps by Theophano.
claims.note: A rumour repeated by chroniclers. Others blamed his hard living. There is no evidence either way.

reigns.hook: Romanos is dead, his sons are tiny and his widow is alone with an unpopular minister. Out east, the army hails Nikephoros Phokas as emperor, and he heads for the capital.

reigns.tagline: The monkish warrior murdered by his wife's lover
reigns.previously: Romanos II dies at 24, leaving a young widow and two small sons.
paragraphs: Nikephoros Phokas was the empire's best general and looked it: stocky, dark and grim. His troops proclaimed him emperor in July 963, and in August he entered Constantinople and was crowned. A month later he married the widowed Theophano and kept her sons, Basil and Constantine, as junior co-emperors. He was close to the monks of Mount Athos and lived like one himself.

He kept winning. Tarsus and the rest of Cilicia fell in 965, and so did Cyprus. In 969 his men took Antioch, Roman again for the first time in over three centuries. But wars cost money. He squeezed taxes, bread prices soared, and his brother Leo was accused of profiteering on grain. In 968 he hosted a western envoy, Liudprand of Cremona, who went home and wrote a savagely rude account of him.

Meanwhile Theophano had fallen for Nikephoros's own nephew, the dashing general John Tzimiskes. On a snowy December night in 969, John and his friends were hauled up the palace wall in a basket and let in. They found Nikephoros asleep on the floor, beat him, and killed him.

claims.text: Nikephoros slept on the floor on an animal skin and wore a hair shirt.
claims.note: Leo the Deacon reports his ascetic habits. They fit his friendship with monks, but may be pious embroidery.

claims.text: The killers were lifted up the palace wall in a basket, with Theophano's help.
claims.note: Told by Leo the Deacon and Skylitzes. Theophano's part was widely believed; she was exiled but never tried.

claims.text: Liudprand called him a pygmy with tiny mole-like eyes.
claims.note: It's in Liudprand's own report of his 968 embassy, written in fury after a miserable visit. It's insult, not portraiture.

reigns.hook: Nikephoros lies dead on his bedroom floor and his killer sits on the throne. But the patriarch won't crown a murderer without a price, and Theophano may be it.

reigns.tagline: The charming killer who became a model emperor
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew and killer of Nikephoros II
reigns.previously: Nikephoros II is murdered in his bedroom by his nephew John.
paragraphs: John Tzimiskes came from a noble family of Armenian descent. He was short, fair, charming and a superb soldier, and he had just killed his uncle. The patriarch Polyeuktos refused to crown him until he did penance, handed over his fellow killers and sent Theophano into exile. John agreed to all of it. To tie himself to the old dynasty, he married Theodora, a daughter of Constantine VII.

Then came the Rus. Prince Sviatoslav of Kiev had overrun Bulgaria and fancied more. In 971 John marched north, took the Bulgarian capital Preslav and penned Sviatoslav inside Dorostolon on the Danube for three months. The Rus gave up and went home, and Pechenegs killed Sviatoslav on the way. Eastern Bulgaria became Byzantine. In 972 John's niece Theophanu married the young western emperor Otto II.

In 975 John swept deep into Syria, taking town after town. On the way home he fell ill, and he died in Constantinople in January 976. Rumour blamed the eunuch Basil Lekapenos, who feared John would look into his land grabs. The throne went back to the dynasty, to Romanos II's sons.

claims.text: Sviatoslav met John with a shaved head, one long lock of hair and a single earring.
claims.note: Leo the Deacon wrote it as if he had seen the meeting. He probably relied on officers who were there.

claims.text: John could leap over four horses standing in a row.
claims.note: One of Leo the Deacon's admiring stories about his strength and agility.

claims.text: Basil Lekapenos poisoned John.
claims.note: Leo the Deacon and Skylitzes report the rumour. A camp fever is just as likely.

reigns.hook: John is dead. Basil II, now about 18, is senior emperor, but his great-uncle the eunuch still holds the reins, and two ambitious generals named Bardas are about to rebel.

reigns.tagline: The grim bachelor who blinded an army
reigns.cameToPower: Senior emperor when John I died
reigns.previously: John Tzimiskes dies suddenly. The crown returns to Romanos II's sons.
paragraphs: Basil had been a co-emperor since he was a toddler, with his younger brother Constantine VIII beside him. Constantine liked parties. Basil liked power. At first his great-uncle, the eunuch Basil Lekapenos, ran things, while the general Bardas Skleros rebelled from 976. Basil threw the eunuch out in 985, then marched on Bulgaria and was humiliated in an ambush at Trajan's Gate in 986.

In 987 another general, Bardas Phokas, revolted. Desperate, Basil turned to Vladimir of Kiev, who sent warriors, the core of the future Varangian Guard, and married Basil's sister Anna after being baptised. That was how the Rus became Christian. In 989 Phokas charged at Basil's lines at Abydos, then dropped dead from his horse. Basil was finally his own master.

He spent years grinding down Samuel of Bulgaria. At Kleidion in 1014 he trapped Samuel's army and blinded the prisoners, leaving one man in each hundred an eye to lead the rest home. Bulgaria was annexed by 1018. Basil never married and had no children, but he left a treasury stuffed with gold. When he died in 1025, the crown passed to his ageing brother.

claims.text: Basil blinded some 14,000 to 15,000 prisoners after Kleidion.
claims.note: The figure comes from Skylitzes, writing decades later. Most historians think it is inflated.

claims.text: Samuel collapsed at the sight of his blinded men and died soon after.
claims.note: Skylitzes tells it. Samuel did die in October 1014, but the deathbed drama may be literary.

claims.text: Nobody called him the Bulgar-Slayer in his lifetime.
claims.note: The nickname is first found in the 12th century and caught on much later, as Paul Stephenson has shown.

reigns.hook: Basil is gone and his brother Constantine VIII, 65 and idle, finally rules. He has no son, only daughters, and the middle one, Zoe, is about to become the most valuable bride in the world.

reigns.title: Zoe's Emperors
reigns.tagline: Father, husband, husband, adopted son: Zoe's men
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother of Basil II, then in-laws
reigns.reignEnded: Michael V blinded by a mob
reigns.previously: Basil II dies unmarried. His idle brother Constantine VIII rules.
paragraphs: Constantine VIII (1025–1028) spent his three years feasting, hunting and blinding anyone he suspected. Dying, he grabbed the city prefect Romanos Argyros, made him leave his wife and marry Zoe, then about 50. Romanos III (1028–1034) dreamed of being a philosopher-king like Marcus Aurelius. His army fled in panic near Aleppo in 1030, though his general George Maniakes took Edessa in 1031.

Zoe had a lover, a handsome young man from Paphlagonia called Michael. In April 1034 Romanos was found dead in his bath, and Zoe married Michael the same day. Michael IV (1034–1041) suffered from epilepsy, so his brother John the Orphanotrophos, a eunuch, ran the state. Harald Hardrada served in the Varangian Guard, and Michael crushed Peter Delyan's Bulgarian revolt in 1041.

Zoe had adopted John's nephew, another Michael. Michael V (1041–1042), nicknamed the Caulker after his father's old trade, turned on her. In April 1042 he had her shorn as a nun and shipped off to an island. Constantinople exploded. The crowds brought Zoe back, fetched her sister Theodora from her convent, and dragged Michael V from a church to be blinded.

claims.text: Romanos III was drowned in his bath on the orders of Zoe and Michael.
claims.note: Psellos, who was at court, hints strongly that he was held under, but stops short of saying it outright.

claims.text: Harald Hardrada, later king of Norway, served in the Varangian Guard.
claims.note: The Norse sagas tell it at length, and the Byzantine writer Kekaumenos confirms that “Araltes” served the emperors.

claims.text: Michael V and his uncle were blinded in front of a jeering crowd.
claims.note: Psellos was there and describes it as an eyewitness.

reigns.hook: Michael V is blind and finished. For the first time ever, two women, the sisters Zoe and Theodora, sit side by side on the throne. They can't stand each other.

reigns.title: Zoe and Theodora
reigns.tagline: Two sisters, one throne, no love lost
reigns.previously: The city rises; Michael V is blinded and Zoe is brought back.
paragraphs: Zoe and Theodora were the last of Basil I's line, the daughters of Constantine VIII. Zoe, the elder, was about 64 and still vain about her looks. Theodora had spent years shut in a convent, partly thanks to her sister. Now the crowd that had toppled Michael V wanted them both, and for the first time in the empire's history two women ruled together.

For seven weeks it more or less worked. They held audiences side by side, sacked Michael's men and gave out justice. Psellos watched them closely. Zoe, he says, turned her rooms into a perfume workshop and kept a face without a wrinkle. She was generous to a fault. Theodora was sharper, plainer and tight with money.

It could not last. The sisters disliked each other, and the court split behind them. Zoe settled it in her own way: she would marry again. Her choice was an old flame, Constantine Monomachos, a charming aristocrat living in exile on Lesbos.

claims.text: Zoe still had a smooth, unlined face in her sixties.
claims.note: Psellos saw her often, but a courtier's flattery is hard to separate from fact.

claims.text: Zoe boiled up perfumes and ointments in her private rooms.
claims.note: Psellos describes the braziers and jars he saw there.

claims.text: This was the only time two women ruled the empire jointly.
claims.note: No other pair of empresses ever ruled together in their own right.

reigns.hook: Zoe is 64 and about to marry for the third time. Her new husband is coming back from exile, and he's bringing his mistress with him.

reigns.tagline: The pleasure-loving emperor of the Great Schism
reigns.previously: Zoe and Theodora rule for seven weeks. Zoe picks a third husband.
paragraphs: Constantine Monomachos was handsome, witty and fond of a good time. He married Zoe on 11 June 1042, then brought in his mistress, Maria Skleraina, gave her a title and rooms in the palace, and the three of them lived together. Zoe seemed not to mind. The people did: in 1044 a crowd rioted, shouting that they wanted no Skleraina as empress.

Trouble came from every side. The great general George Maniakes rebelled in 1043 and was killed at the moment of victory. A Rus fleet attacked the same year and was beaten off. In 1045 Constantine annexed the Armenian kingdom of Ani. In 1047 the rebel Leo Tornikios besieged the capital and nearly got in. Constantine also founded a law school, run by Psellos's friend John Xiphilinos.

Zoe died in 1050. In 1054 a row with Rome boiled over. On 16 July the papal envoy Cardinal Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch Michael Keroularios hit back in kind. That split, the Great Schism, still divides the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Constantine died in January 1055.

claims.text: Maria Skleraina lived openly in the palace with an official title.
claims.note: Psellos, who served Constantine, describes the arrangement closely. Her title was sebaste.

claims.text: Humbert laid the bull on the altar of Hagia Sophia on 16 July 1054.
claims.note: Recorded in both Greek and Latin documents from the time.

claims.text: In the Hagia Sophia mosaic, Constantine's face replaced an earlier husband's.
claims.note: The heads and his name were clearly altered. Many think it first showed Romanos III, but nobody can be sure.

reigns.hook: Constantine IX is dead. His advisers have picked a successor, but old Theodora, last of the Macedonians, is not finished yet.

reigns.tagline: The spinster empress who closed a 190-year dynasty
reigns.previously: Constantine IX dies in 1055, months after the Great Schism.
paragraphs: Theodora had spent much of her life in convents and in her sister's shadow. After sharing the throne with Zoe for a few weeks in 1042, she stepped back. As Constantine IX lay dying, his advisers planned to pass the crown to Nikephoros Proteuon, the governor of Bulgaria. Theodora moved first. Her supporters got her to the Great Palace and she was proclaimed empress.

In her seventies and unmarried, she ruled alone and would not take a husband. She worked through trusted officials, chiefly her minister Leo Paraspondylos, and made appointments herself, even in the Church. Psellos grumbled that it was unnatural for a woman to rule, but the empire was quiet.

In August 1056 she fell ill. On her deathbed her advisers had her name an elderly official, Michael Bringas, as her successor. She died on 31 August 1056. The dynasty that Basil the groom had founded almost 190 years earlier was over.

claims.text: Theodora barely took part in choosing Michael VI; her inner circle did it.
claims.note: Psellos says the decision was made by her advisers while she was too ill to speak.

claims.text: She was the last ruler descended from Basil I.
claims.note: With her death the Macedonian dynasty ended, and no one else had a hereditary claim.

reigns.hook: Theodora is dead and her dynasty with her. The new emperor is an old civil servant, and the generals are running out of patience.

reigns.title: Generals and Bureaucrats
reigns.tagline: Pen-pushers and soldiers take turns on the throne
reigns.cameToPower: Deathbed pick, revolt, then a handover
reigns.reignEnded: Constantine X dies in his bed
reigns.previously: Old Theodora dies, naming the elderly official Michael Bringas.
paragraphs: Michael VI (1056–1057) was a veteran civil servant. At Easter 1057 the top generals came to court hoping for rewards and he sent them away with a scolding. In June they proclaimed one of their own, Isaac Komnenos. After Isaac's army beat the loyalists near Nicaea, Michael was talked into stepping down and became a monk.

Isaac I Komnenos (1057–1059) was a hard soldier who wanted to fix the treasury fast. His gold coins showed him holding a drawn sword. He fell out badly with the mighty patriarch Michael Keroularios and had him arrested. Then, ill and fed up, he abdicated in late 1059, retired to a monastery and handed the crown to Constantine Doukas.

Constantine X Doukas (1059–1067) was a courtier's emperor who saved money by starving the army. Meanwhile the Seljuk Turks took the great Armenian city of Ani in 1064, and the Uzes, nomads from the steppe, flooded over the Danube. When Constantine died in May 1067, his widow Eudokia Makrembolitissa took charge for their young sons.

claims.text: Michael VI publicly humiliated the generals at Easter 1057, driving them to revolt.
claims.note: Michael Psellos was at court and tells the story, though he liked to make himself central to events.

claims.text: Isaac's sword-holding coins meant he credited his throne to his own blade instead of to God.
claims.note: The coins are real. The boastful meaning is how later chroniclers read them; it may just be a soldier's image.

claims.text: Eudokia swore in writing never to remarry, to protect her sons' rights.
claims.note: Psellos and other writers mention the oath, which was lodged with the patriarch. She broke it within months.

reigns.hook: Eudokia has sworn not to remarry. But the Turks are raiding deep into Anatolia, and in the cells sits a handsome general condemned for plotting. She has a better use for him.

reigns.tagline: The emperor the sultan stepped on, then sent home
reigns.previously: Constantine X dies. His widow Eudokia rules for their young sons.
paragraphs: Romanos Diogenes was a tough Cappadocian general who had been sentenced for plotting against Eudokia's sons. She pardoned him, broke her oath and married him on 1 January 1068. The Doukas family, led by Constantine X's brother John, the Caesar, never forgave either of them. Romanos set about rebuilding a neglected army and led it east against the Turks.

In 1071 he marched a huge, patchy army to Manzikert, near Lake Van, to meet Sultan Alp Arslan. On 26 August, as the line pulled back at dusk, the rearguard under Andronikos Doukas, the Caesar's son, marched off the field. Romanos fought on until he was wounded and taken. Brought before the sultan, he was treated with honour and freed after about a week, with a treaty.

He came home to find himself deposed. The Doukas clan had crowned Eudokia's son as Michael VII. Romanos fought and lost, then surrendered on a sworn promise of safety. In 1072 he was blinded anyway, and died of the wounds in a monastery on the island of Prote.

claims.text: Andronikos Doukas betrayed Romanos on purpose at Manzikert.
claims.note: Attaleiates, who was there, says the rearguard spread a rumour the emperor had lost. Whether it was a planned betrayal is argued.

claims.text: Alp Arslan put his foot on the captured emperor's neck, then raised him up and treated him kindly.
claims.note: The foot on the neck was a ritual of triumph described by Muslim writers. Byzantine sources stress the kindness. The details vary a lot.

claims.text: Psellos wrote to the blinded Romanos calling him blessed, as if losing his eyes were a gift from God.
claims.note: A letter of Psellos to Romanos survives; how cruel or sincere it was is debated. Psellos backed the Doukas side.

reigns.hook: Romanos is blind and dying. In the capital, Psellos's star pupil sits on the throne, and the Turks have learned that nobody is guarding Anatolia.

reigns.title: After Manzikert
reigns.tagline: Ten years of losing Anatolia and the plot
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Doukas family takes back the throne
reigns.reignEnded: The Komnenos brothers storm the city
reigns.previously: Romanos is captured at Manzikert, freed, then deposed and blinded.
paragraphs: Michael VII Doukas (1071–1078) was Psellos's pupil, bookish and no soldier. People called him Parapinakes, "minus a quarter", because his gold coin bought a quarter less wheat. His minister Nikephoritzes squeezed everyone. Turkish bands spread over Anatolia, and the Norman mercenary Roussel de Bailleul rebelled with his knights until a young officer, Alexios Komnenos, caught him.

In 1077 two generals called Nikephoros revolted at once: Bryennios in the Balkans and Botaneiates in Anatolia. In March 1078 Michael gave up and became a monk. Old Nikephoros III Botaneiates (1078–1081) took the city and married Michael's wife, the beautiful Maria of Alania, though Michael was alive. Alexios Komnenos beat Bryennios for him, then waited.

In southern Italy the Norman duke Robert Guiscard was planning an invasion, with a man claiming to be the deposed Michael VII. In early 1081 the Komnenos brothers, Isaac and Alexios, slipped out of the capital and raised the army. On 1 April 1081 they got into Constantinople through a gate held by German mercenaries, and their troops looted the city.

claims.text: The nickname Parapinakes came from the coin buying a quarter-measure less wheat.
claims.note: Chroniclers explain it this way, and prices did rise under Michael VII while the coin was debased.

claims.text: Robert Guiscard paraded a fake Michael VII to justify invading.
claims.note: Anna Komnene says the pretender was a monk named Raiktor; other sources agree there was a pretender. Anna mocks him, so the details are coloured.

claims.text: Maria of Alania backed the Komnenos coup in secret.
claims.note: Anna Komnene, who had good reason to flatter the family, hints at it. Maria did adopt Alexios as a son.

reigns.hook: The city is looted and Botaneiates is in a monastery. The new emperor is a soldier of about 24 with an empty treasury, and Robert Guiscard's Normans are about to land.
